title: Strategy Induction: Control Primitives as Emergent Properties of Sufficiently Hierarchical World Modeling

html:
The previous section fleshed out the nature of reasoning and argued that it relies on and is directly derived from lower- and middle-order representations. This section collapses the "representational" and "control" distinction (without claiming the distinction is useless/invalid) since it will allow us to more clearly explain how humans learn to design, pursue, and attain long-term goals whole responding flexibly and adaptively to changes in the environment.

We show that attention control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory are distinct but they share a common factor. This factor is completely identical with an integral construct standing for relational integration and awareness, suggesting that executive function does not have much beyond this construct 1

Control primitives are definitely enabled by sufficiently hierarchical world modeling (since they involve abstract representations) but are they actually an emergent phenomenon or were abstract representations evolutionarily optimized to have a high "control coefficient" (influence on the rest of the brain)? Or, given the nature/constraints of the brain (the learning rules and architecture), would abstract representations have to have a high control coefficient to exist in the first place?

Thinking is another form of control

Learning by thinking in natural and artificial minds

From skills to strategies

Cognitive control

a family of top-down mental processes needed when you have to concentrate and pay attention, when going on automatic or relying on instinct or intuition would be ill-advised, insufficient, or impossible 4

a set of processes enabling us to design, pursue, and attain short- and long-term goals while responding flexibly and adaptively to changes in the environment 5

We can (partially) collapse the distinction between cortical regions underlying "representation" and those underlying "control", making every cortical region a "representation of the environment that is necessarily action-oriented, with information integration occurring across varying timescales". While "control" and "representational" regions certainly have their distinctions besides their intrinsic timescales and representational contents (e.g region-specific connectivity to subcortical regions and neuromodulatory hubs), by seeing cognitive control as the natural dynamics of the most abstract, temporally extended layers of the hierarchical world model, this allows us to better explain how executive functions are learned 6.

This is what the active inference folks argue; they unify perception and action under one objective: Minimizing Free Energy. All cognition is "goal-directed" because the brain is always trying to minimize the divergence between its model and reality, contrasting popular definitions of executive functions as cognitive processes that underlie "goal-directed behavior" 7; labeling EFs as those cognitive functions underlying goal-directed behavior. The field of active inference still uses the term to distinguish between Model-Based (calculating the path to a goal state) and Habitual/Amortized (reflexive State→ActionState \rightarrow Action mappings), but they still are just two ways of doing the same thing (minimizing surprise).

If the brain is a hierarchical generative model, the higher layers must encode slower, more stable latent variables (context, rules, plans). This recent study illustrates figure 2. The spacetime attractor (Figure) 14. This recent study illustrates figure 3. STA dynamics and fixed points (Figure).

Mapping each executive function

Inhibitory control: involves being able to control one’s attention, behavior, thoughts, and/or emotions to override a strong internal predisposition or external lure, and instead do what’s more appropriate or needed 4

Inhibition maps to Action Selection/Policy Arbitration: The competition between the high-level policy and the low-level policy. "Inhibition" is not a force that pushes back; it is the act of assigning extremely high precision (confidence) to a top-down prior ("I am a person who remains calm") relative to the bottom-up sensory/proprioceptive prediction error ("I am about to punch this person").

Shifting (Flexibility): one aspect is being able to change perspectives spatially (e.g., "What would this look like if I viewed it from a different direction?") or interpersonally (e.g., "Let me see if I can see this from your point of view"). To change perspectives, we need to inhibit (or deactivate) our previous perspective and load into WM (or activate) a different perspective. It is in this sense that cognitive flexibility requires and builds on inhibitory control and WM. Another aspect of cognitive flexibility involves changing how we think about something (thinking outside the box). For example, if one way of solving a problem isn’t working, can we come up with a new way of attacking this or conceiving of this that hadn’t been considered before? Cognitive flexibility also involves being flexible enough to adjust to changed demands or priorities, to admit you were wrong, and to take advantage of sudden, unexpected opportunities. Suppose you were planning to do X, but an amazing opportunity arose to do Y: Do you have the flexibility to take advantage of serendipity?

maps to State Transition/Inference: The ability of the high-level model to rapidly switch its belief about which "context" (latent state) is currently active. If your model is "sticky" (low flexibility), it over-predicts the previous context.

Working memory: involves holding information in mind and mentally working with it (or said differently, working with information no longer perceptually present 4

Updating (WM) maps to State Maintenance: The stability of the active high-level representation over time. Lower levels of the brain (sensory cortex) encode fast-changing variables (milliseconds). Higher levels (PFC) encode slow-changing latent variables (seconds/minutes). When you "hold" a thought, you aren’t storing it; your high-level model is stuck in a stable state that predicts a sequence of lower-level dynamics. The "maintenance" is just the natural inertia of a high-level representation that has a slow time constant.

Metacognition = Hyperpriors (Beliefs about Beliefs): This is the system estimating its own uncertainty. It’s not just predicting the world; it’s predicting how precise its predictions are likely to be. It is abstracting over learning episodes and thought processes themselves. It’s not just predicting the world; it’s predicting how precise its predictions are likely to be.

Reasons why removing the distinction between "representational" and "control" regions is useful

The same machinery (i.e cortical columns) that comes to be used to discover hierarchical representations requiring low and middling abstraction (e.g basic fine/gross motor control, classification, and navigation) can to some extent be naively extended and give rise to abstract representations (and executive functions)

Labeling certain regions as "control" or "executive" regions is still useful:

Calling certain regions "working memory regions" (i.e dlPFC) is useful because these are indeed the regions that maintain their activity over the longest time periods and contain the variables that most directly correlate with our behaviors; however, these regions can equivalently be seen as the regions that simply model the most higher-order/low-frequency (abstract) variables, which leads to particularly auto-correlated representations over time and just so happen to be the representations that maximize cumulative rewards (explaining their acquired "top-down influence" across development).

Executive functions are not control primitives but emergent properties of high-level generative models constraining lower-level perception, valuation, and action; it simply turns on when higher order patterns/rules/representations are present, especially those that haven’t been fully internalized into ventral striatal policies

Can I conceptualize executive functions essentially as the most abstract portion of the world model? Each executive fucntion just seems like the natural behavioral/cognitive signature of higher-order pattern recognition. For example, "inhibition" is recognized when you realize the more concrete parts of your brain are incorrect in their valuation of an action due to them missing some higher-order pattern ("I shouldn’t call her a bitch cause I have X higher-order goal to reach"). Working memory maintanence is merely a reflection of the fact that abstract patterns/rules/representations necessarily have "slots" that lower-order patterns fit into. Metacognition is the highest-order abstract knowledge, where self and thought are themselves abstracted (other executive functions + internal states are abstracted). The label of executive function being "goal-directed" seems like a useless label, as all cognition is goal-directed (used to think this, but "goal-directed" needs to be altered to "long term goal-directed" to make sense as a classifier for EFs).

It is quite integrative, and therefore quite costly to run. Consciousness is expensive!

Prefrontal cortex sits at the apex of a representational hierarchy: long temporal receptive fields, high abstraction, multimodal integration, and weak coupling to immediate sensory input.

When a high-level latent variable becomes active - a long-horizon goal, social rule, identity constraint, or abstract task structure - it necessarily re-weights downstream value functions, policies, and attentional priorities. What psychologists label as "executive function" is just what this re-weighting looks like behaviorally.

Planning, skills, and hierarchical control

Executive function (expressed component-wise) can be seen as the principal limiter from an early age; develops extremely slowly and is both a key enabler of and a key beneficiary of post-training

The competence system is concerned with understanding or knowing, whereas the procedural system makes success possible on particular problems (Overton, 1990; Overton & Dick, 2007). Performance or procedural factors cannot substitute for competence, and the latter cannot be reduced to some set of procedures. The competence system for formal reasoning in Overton’s account is assumed to consist of a mental logic that resembles standard propositional logic. see Overton and colleague’s "competence-procedural" theory

executive function as a bottleneck on conceptual change. Susan B Carey and collaborators show that the ability to update intuitive theories depends on working memory, inhibition, and cognitive flexibility: children must hold competing representations in mind, inhibit default interpretations, and switch between explanatory frameworks as they test new hypotheses

Looking deeper into the algorithms underlying human planning; a mechanistic theory of planning in prefrontal cortex; cognitive maps in prefrontal cortex

Language-parameterized skill library

Treat skill acquisition as the control-theoretic side of abstraction. Start with corticostriatal loops as a library builder: dorsomedial circuits learn flexible, goal-directed policies; dorsolateral circuits slowly crystallize habits/options; ventral loops set vigor and motivation. Explain how subgoal discovery arises from bottlenecks in the state-transition graph (frontoparietal discovery, striatal consolidation) and how chunking shows up in neural population dynamics as low-dimensional, reusable trajectories. Fold in the cerebellum as a supervised calibrator of forward/inverse models for each skill, emphasizing vector-valued teaching lines from inferior olive that tune timing and gains. End with the robotics-ready pattern: discover options via graph bottlenecks or successor-eigenoptions, pretrain cerebellum-like inverse models with dense supervised traces, and use BG-like distributional critics to stitch skills together with risk-aware arbitration.

Learning Reasoning and Rationality from Everyday Experiences: Discovering Strategies and Abstractions

Derive a full spec for how reasoning is learned

From skills to strategies; from strategies to systems of strategies

Awake replay: off the clock but on the job

Learning by thinking in natural and artificial minds

Embodied cognition perspectives within early executive function development

How is reasoning learned? It seems like humans may never learn them without cultural technology (which allows humans across millenia to essentially function as a super-organism, increasing the sample efficiency of each successive generation), but that there is also a strong RL component (mostly on-policy but also offline/off-policy)

First, there are some proto-strategies that you probably get "for free" from generic learning machinery. If you drop a kid in a rich environment with no schooling, they still discover things like "try another way if the first attempt fails," "compare this situation to a remembered similar one," "mentally test a few steps ahead before acting," and "look for where the difference is between two conditions." You can think of these as primitive internal options over a world model. The brain’s RL system is not just tuning motor outputs; it’s tuning policies over internal computations: where to attend, whether to simulate, how many steps to roll out, whether to check an alternative hypothesis. When a particular mini-procedure reliably improves reward (solving puzzles faster, avoiding scolding, getting praise, experiencing that "aha" intrinsic reward), it gets reinforced as a reusable pattern.

Second, there’s an explicit RL story over strategies, not just actions. Take "try a counterexample" as a reasoning mode. Initially a child might occasionally think, "wait, is there a case where this doesn’t work?" by accident. When that move pays off-by catching an error on homework, impressing a teacher, winning an argument-it gets value. Over many episodes, the control system learns something like: in states with features abstract claim, high stakes, moderate time, prior conflict, launch the "search for counterexample" routine. That’s on-policy meta-RL over their own reasoning: each episode is "I tried strategy S in context C and got reward R." Offline/off-policy kicks in when they replay episodes in memory or imagine how things could have gone ("if I’d checked both cases, I wouldn’t have been wrong") and assign credit or blame retroactively; hippocampal replay plus prefrontal evaluation is doing gradient steps on a policy over internal operations rather than just overt behavior.

Now add culture, and everything explodes in richness and sample efficiency. Other people literally present you with high-performing internal policies: "When you’re stuck, draw a diagram"; "Consider the opposite hypothesis"; "Prove it by contradiction"; "Control one variable at a time." Instruction, worked examples, and even casual language ("what if everyone did that?", "in the extreme case…") are all ways of shipping pre-discovered reasoning modes into your head. Mechanistically, that looks like a mix of imitation learning (copying external verbalized chains of thought), supervised learning (matching teacher solutions), and RL (praise, grades, not-looking-stupid in front of peers). Crucially, culture doesn’t just give you strategies, it gives you meta-tags and cues: "this is a proof by induction," "this is a thought experiment," which helps the control system learn a mapping from problem features -> appropriate mode much faster than unguided exploration would.

There’s also a strong offline/off-policy component via text, lectures, and examples. When you read a proof or watch someone debug, you’re seeing a trajectory in "reasoning space" that you didn’t generate. You can still update your own policy: "In problems of type T, the experts open with step X, not step Y." That’s off-policy learning over internal actions: you’re adjusting which mental steps you would take in a state, based on someone else’s trace. This is exactly why cultural technology (writing, notation, diagrams, formal logic, algebra, probability theory) is so powerful: it externalizes sequences of internal operations so they can be observed, copied, tweaked, and recombined by others.

Over time, repeated use and reward turn some of these modes from slow, effortful System-2 procedures into fast, semi-automatic System-1 patterns. Early on, "do a case split" is a deliberate choice; later, the space of cases just pops into mind. The basal ganglia-PFC loop is basically learning which internal option to gate in which context and how long to run it. Additionally, metacognition itself becomes a learned strategy library: "If my confidence is low but stakes are high, escalate to a more expensive mode (formal check, external calculation, ask for help)." That’s reflective-system RL over which algorithmic patterns to deploy.
